content.title: Improving Experimental Reliability and Validity
content.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying and correcting experimental design flaws to ensure that results are accurate (valid) and consistent (reliable). The primary strategy involves controlling confounding variables to isolate the effect of the independent variable.
learning_objectives: Distinguish between experimental validity and reliability.
Identify confounding variables that differ between experimental groups.
Select modifications that control non-manipulated variables to improve validity.
Recognize how standardized measurement procedures enhance reliability.

sections.title: Validity vs. Reliability
sections.content: Validity refers to the accuracy of an experiment—whether it actually measures what it claims to measure. An experiment is valid if the observed changes in the dependent variable are caused solely by the independent variable. Reliability refers to the consistency of results. If an experiment is repeated under the same conditions and yields the same results, it is reliable. Increasing sample size or repeating measurements typically improves reliability, while controlling variables improves validity.

sections.title: Identifying and Controlling Confounds
sections.content:
A confounding variable (or confound) is a non-manipulated factor that differs between experimental groups and could influence the outcome. To improve validity, researchers must 'match' these variables, making them identical across all groups. This ensures that the independent variable is the only difference between the groups. Common confounds include differences in materials (e.g., soil type), environment (e.g., temperature), or timing (e.g., duration of exposure).

![A flowchart showing the steps to improve experimental validity: Identify Confounds, Match Variables, and Standardize Tools.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/b414f1a5-1008-45fd-b1f4-ad00374d8551-1786506684985-295.webp)

sections.title: Standardizing Procedures
sections.content: Reliability and validity are both supported by standardized procedures. This means using the same tools, the same measurement units, and the same schedules for every subject in the study. If one group is measured with a digital scale and another with a spring scale, the difference in tool precision introduces a confound that threatens the validity of the comparison.

worked_examples.question: A researcher wants to test if a new fertilizer increases tomato yield. Group A (Fertilizer) is kept in a greenhouse at 75°F and watered daily. Group B (No Fertilizer) is kept outdoors where temperatures fluctuate and is watered every three days. Which modification would best improve the validity of this experiment?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the independent variable (Fertilizer). Step 2: Identify non-manipulated variables that differ between groups (Location/Temperature and Watering Schedule). Step 3: Apply the 'Match and Control' strategy. To isolate the effect of the fertilizer, both groups must be kept in the same location (e.g., both in the greenhouse) and follow the exact same watering schedule. This ensures that any difference in tomato yield is due to the fertilizer, not the temperature or water.

common_mistakes: Confusing sample size with validity: Increasing the number of subjects (n) improves reliability and statistical power, but it does not fix a fundamental design flaw like a confounding variable.

Randomization as a total fix: While random assignment helps distribute unknown biases, it does not replace the need to actively control known environmental variables like light, temperature, or soil type.
Ignoring measurement tools: Using different rulers or scales for different groups is a common 'hidden' confound in ACT Science passages.
exam_tips: If a question asks for the 'best' way to improve a comparison, look for the answer choice that makes the groups more similar in every way except for the independent variable.
Watch for 'procedural' differences mentioned in the text, such as one group being tested in the morning and another in the evening.
Validity = 'Is this a fair test?'; Reliability = 'Are these results consistent?'
content.recap: To improve experimental validity, identify any variable other than the independent variable that differs between groups and make those variables identical. To improve reliability, standardize measurement tools and increase the number of trials or subjects.

knowledge_claims.content: Validity is the extent to which an experiment accurately measures the effect of the independent variable without interference from confounds.
Reliability is the consistency of experimental results when measurements are repeated or sample sizes are increased.
A confounding variable is any non-manipulated factor that differs between experimental groups and could influence the dependent variable.
To improve validity, non-manipulated variables that differ between groups must be made identical (matched) across all groups.
In a valid experimental design, only the independent variable should differ between the experimental and control groups.
Standardizing measurement procedures involves using the same tools, timing, and units for all groups to prevent measurement bias.
Increasing the sample size (number of subjects) improves reliability but does not correct validity issues caused by confounding variables.
A design is flawed if the groups use different materials, such as different soil types in a plant growth study, unless soil is the independent variable.
If two groups are measured with different instruments (e.g., different rulers), the best fix is to measure all subjects using the same instrument.
Results are considered more reliable when multiple trials yield consistent data points or when averages are taken from larger datasets.
While randomization reduces selection bias, active control of environmental variables is required to eliminate physical confounds.
Differences in watering schedules, light exposure, or temperature between groups are common confounds in biological experiments.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 1: Enzyme Activity Across pH
Researchers measured the activity of an enzyme from two microorganisms across four buffer pH values. Equal enzyme concentrations and substrate amounts were used. Activity is reported as micromoles of product formed per minute.

Which statement correctly identifies variables in the study?

options.F: The measured outcome was held constant in every trial.
options.G: No condition was intentionally varied or classified.
options.H: Buffer pH was the independent variable and product formation rate was the dependent variable.
options.J: The graph title was the dependent variable.

items.explanation: The correct choice distinguishes the factor varied or classified from the outcome measured.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 2: Mulch and Soil Infiltration
Students packed identical soil columns and applied simulated rain. Experiment 1 compared bare soil with 2 cm and 5 cm layers of straw mulch. They measured water collected below each column after 20 minutes. Experiment 2 repeated the treatments after gently compacting the soil.

Which choice correctly identifies the independent variable(s) in the investigation?

options.C: soil mass, rainfall rate, and collection time
options.D: the numerical labels printed on the graph

items.explanation: Independent variables are intentionally varied or used to define treatment conditions.

videoLesson.title: Select Controls to Improve Validity
videoLesson.description: Recognize non-manipulated variables that differ between groups as potential confounds. Make those variables identical across groups and record remaining differences as controls.
